# Problem as-is
Documentation hides detail such that user need to find out failing cases by oneself.
Specifically, implementation vs. documentation as follows:
- `dot_scaled` requires `rhs_k_pack=True` for FP4 inputs
  - both for MXFP4 and NVFP4
  - for most of Blackwells (test required for GB100, GB200, etc.)
- documentation does not state that

## Specifically
`dot_scaled` on CUDA with FP4 input require `rhs_k_pack=True` (the default value)
Current test cases clearly shows that:
- [This case](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/7c56a5e40f7fd928dfd5c72902d5def0097db73a/python/test/unit/language/test_matmul.py#L990)  for NVFP4
- [This case](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/7c56a5e40f7fd928dfd5c72902d5def0097db73a/python/test/unit/language/test_matmul.py#L994) for MXFP4 and NVFP4 on SM120

Personally tested `dot_scaled` with MXFP4 input and `rhs_k_pack=False`.
It fails during MLIR passes with input shape error as follows:

```
python3: /project/third_party/nvidia/lib/TritonNVIDIAGPUToLLVM/DotOpToLLVM/MMAv2.cpp:760:
LogicalResult (anonymous namespace)::convertMMAImpl(
  DotOpInterface, Value, Value, Value,
  const LLVMType Converter *,
  ConversionPatternRewriter &,
  TensorCoreType,
  const NumRegisters &,
  const std::map<TensorCoreType, std::string> &,
  const EmitMmaCallback &
): Assertion `repA[2] == repB[1]' failed.

...

%148 = ttg.local_load %124 : !ttg.memdesc<128x64xi8, #shared, #smem> -> tensor<128x64xi8, #ttg.dot_op<{opIdx = 0, parent = #mma, kWidth = 4}>>
%149 = ttg.local_load %144 : !ttg.memdesc<128x64xi8, #shared1, #smem> -> tensor<128x64xi8, #ttg.dot_op<{opIdx = 1, parent = #mma, kWidth = 4}>>
%150 = ttg.convert_layout %134 : tensor<128x4xi8, #blocked1> -> tensor<128x4xi8, #linear>
%151 = ttg.convert_layout %147 : tensor<128x4xi8, #blocked1> -> tensor<128x4xi8, #linear1>

%152 = tt.dot_scaled
  %148 scale %150,  # **lhs 128x64 i8 (128x128 fp4), scale 128x4**
  %149 scale %151,  # **rhs 128x64 i8 (128x128 fp4), scale 128x4**
  %arg14 lhs = e2m1 rhs = e2m1 {fastMath = false, **rhs_k_pack = false**}
:
tensor<128x64xi8, #ttg.dot_op<{opIdx = 0, parent = #mma, kWidth = 4}>>,
tensor<128x4xi8, #linear>
*
tensor<128x64xi8, #ttg.dot_op<{opIdx = 1, parent = #mma, kWidth = 4}>>,
tensor<128x4xi8, #linear1>
-> tensor<128x128xf32, #mma>
scf.yield %152 : tensor<128x128xf32, #mma>
```

# To-be
- documentation ([live doc](https://triton-lang.org/main/python-api/generated/triton.language.dot_scaled.html#triton.language.dot_scaled), [code](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/dbb23f1c707b81af4eda0c17a3f343861c0fd71e/python/triton/language/core.py#L2368)) need to clearly state conditions that `rhs_k_pack=True` is required.

---
Tested environment
- `nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:25.10-py3` container with triton v3.6.0
- Blackwell GB203 (5070Ti)
- compute-capability=120 ptx-version=88
- nvidia-driver-open 580.126.09

I looked through all issues with `dot_scaled`, both open and closed.
Please correct me if I'm wrong.
title: FP4 inputs of `dot_scaled` need more hints on documentation

body:
Dear all,

I am proposing to add documentation for the data types supported by Triton.

Creation ops require a dtype argument from `tl.dtype`. I could not find a list of valid data types in the Triton documentation.

To fix this, a few lines for each type in `tl.dtype` could be added in `triton/language/core.py`. This could be done similarly to the [PyTorch data type documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/tensor_attributes.html#torch-dtype), with a table of supported types and a short description.

If this is something the maintainers would be interested in adding, I could make a pull request with the changes.
title: Add Documentation for Triton Data Types

body:
## Problem
Following the installation instructions fails on fresh Ubuntu systems due to missing system dependencies.

## Error
Could NOT find ZLIB (missing: ZLIB_LIBRARY ZLIB_INCLUDE_DIR)
Could NOT find LibXml2 (missing: LIBXML2_LIBRARY LIBXML2_INCLUDE_DIR)
CMake Generate step failed. Build files cannot be regenerated correctly.


## Reproduction Steps
1. Fresh Ubuntu 22.04 system
2. Install Python 3.12 and create virtual environment
3. Follow README instructions:
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/triton-lang/triton
   cd triton/
   pip install -r python/requirements.txt
   pip install -e . --verbose --no-build-isolation
4.Build fails with ZLIB/LibXml2 errors


## Environment

Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS
Python 3.12.11
NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3
CUDA 12.4

## Solution
Install required system dependencies before triton build:
```bash
sudo apt install zlib1g-dev libxml2-dev build-essential
```


### Proposed Documentation Fix
Add prerequisites section to README.md:

## Prerequisites
### Ubuntu/Debian
```bash
sudo apt install zlib1g-dev libxml2-dev build-essential
```
### CentOS/RHEL
```bash
sudo yum install zlib-devel libxml2-devel gcc gcc-c++
```

This affects new users following the installation guide and prevents successful builds without additional research.
title: Add system dependencies to installation documentation

title: install failed in ubuntu

body:
## Summary

Nightly wheels uploaded to the Azure DevOps `Triton-Nightly` feed use a PEP 440 *local version* of the form `3.7.0+git<commit-hash>`. Because PEP 440 sorts non-numeric local-version segments **lexicographically**, `pip` does not pick the most recently built wheel — it picks the wheel whose commit hash sorts highest as a string. This silently downgrades users who run the documented install command.

## Reproduction

Two recent nightly wheels exist on the feed:

| Build (UTC)            | Commit       | Wheel filename                                             |
|------------------------|--------------|------------------------------------------------------------|
| earlier                | `f97f66ab`   | `triton-3.7.0+gitf97f66ab-cp310-cp310-...whl`              |
| 2026-05-04 ~10:25 (newer) | `886365ca`   | `triton-3.7.0+git886365ca-cp310-cp310-...whl`              |

Run the documented install command:

```bash
pip install triton \
  --index-url https://aiinfra.pkgs.visualstudio.com/PublicPackages/_packaging/Triton-Nightly/pypi/simple/
```

Observed:

```text
$ python -c "import triton; print(triton.__version__)"
3.7.0+gitf97f66ab        # the OLDER commit
```

Expected:

```text
3.7.0+git886365ca        # the most recently built commit
```

## Root cause

[PEP 440 — Local version identifiers](https://peps.python.org/pep-0440/#local-version-identifiers):

> Comparison and ordering of local versions considers each segment of the local version (divided by a `.`) separately. If a segment consists entirely of ASCII digits then that section should be considered for comparison purposes as integer rather than string ordering. If a segment contains any ASCII letters then that segment is compared lexicographically with case insensitivity.

The current local version `git<hash>` is a **single non-numeric segment**, so it is compared as a case-insensitive string:

```python
>>> from packaging.version import Version
>>> Version("3.7.0+gitf97f66ab") > Version("3.7.0+git886365ca")
True   # 'gitf' > 'git8' lexicographically — but 886365ca is the newer commit
```

There is no time component in the version string, so newer commits whose hashes happen to start with `0`–`8` will lose to any older surviving wheel whose hash starts with `9`–`f`.

## Why it matters

- Users who follow the documented install command get an arbitrarily old nightly with no warning.
- Downstream projects that test against the *latest* Triton silently keep testing against a stale build — breaking exactly the early-feedback loop nightlies exist for. We hit this when a feature recently merged upstream (`knobs.autotuning.listener`) was not present in the wheel `pip` selected, even though it was present at the actual newest commit on the feed.
- This is a regression from the historical `triton-nightly` package on the same feed, which used `3.0.0.postYYYYMMDDHHMMSS` and sorted correctly because `.postN` is numeric.

## Proposed fix

Make the local version's first segment a **monotonic numeric timestamp** of the commit date. Suggested format:

```
3.7.0+<UTC-commit-date>.git<short-hash>
e.g. 3.7.0+20260504100016.git886365ca
```

PEP 440 will compare `20260504100016` (numeric) before falling back to the hash, so ordering becomes strictly time-monotonic. The hash is preserved for traceability and `pip install triton==3.7.0+20260504100016.git886365ca` still works for exact pinning.

```python
>>> from packaging.version import Version
>>> Version("3.7.0+20260504100016.git886365ca") > Version("3.7.0+20260503080000.gitf97f66ab")
True   # ✓ time-correct ordering
```

### Implementation sketch

The CI workflow already computes the commit date — see this snippet from the current Build-Wheels job:

```bash
export LATEST_DATE=$(TZ=UTC0 git show --quiet \
  --date='format-local:%Y%m%d%H%M%S' --format="%cd")
```

Two small changes are needed:

1. **`python/setup.py`** (or wherever the version string is assembled): read a `TRITON_BUILD_TIMESTAMP` env var and prepend it to the local-version segment. Fall back to reading the commit date from local `git` so developer builds still produce a sensible version.

2. **`.github/workflows/wheels.yml`**: forward `LATEST_DATE` as `TRITON_BUILD_TIMESTAMP` into the cibuildwheel container via `CIBW_ENVIRONMENT` (plain `export` is not enough — `cibuildwheel` runs the build in a separate manylinux container).

Using the *commit* date (not build wall-clock) means rebuilding the same commit produces the same version string, preserving build reproducibility.


## Compatibility impact of the proposed fix

- ✅ `pip install triton --index-url <feed>` — selects the newest wheel correctly.
- ✅ Coexistence with already-published `+gitXXXX` wheels — old wheels remain installable; new wheels sort above them by virtue of having a numeric leading segment vs a non-numeric one.
- ⚠️ Exact-pin of an already-published hash (`triton==3.7.0+git886365ca`) — would no longer match a newly-rebuilt wheel of the same commit, since the new wheel would be named `+20260504100016.git886365ca`. Hash-pinning is an anti-pattern for nightlies, but should be called out in the release notes.
- ✅ Independent feeds (`pytorch-triton` on download.pytorch.org) — unaffected.

## Side note (not blocking)

The CI step that computes `PACKAGE_DATE` from the existing index uses `grep -oP '(?<=, )[0-9\.]+dev[0-9]+(?=\))'`. That pattern matched the legacy `triton-nightly` `.postN` versions but matches nothing in the current `+git<hash>` scheme — `PACKAGE_DATE` is presumably empty on every run today. Worth updating once the version scheme settles.

## Environment

- Triton feed: `https://aiinfra.pkgs.visualstudio.com/PublicPackages/_packaging/Triton-Nightly/pypi/simple/`
- Build job: `Build-Wheels (self-hosted, CPU, x86_64)` from triton-lang/triton, run 2026-05-04
- Latest commit at time of report: `886365ca82b03edef597b0d2c8c32be62ac2546b` ("[Proton] Normalize roofline metric dtypes")
- pip / packaging versions: pip 25.x, packaging 25.0 (any version that implements PEP 440 sorting reproduces this)

body:
When `cache_results` is set for `@triton.autotune` autotune timings are cached to disk to avoid future autotuning, but in the current implementation they are all cached as a single file and the cache key includes the list of configs. This means if you add or remove a config from your autotune list (or alter your `prune_configs_by`) Triton reruns all the autotuning. I propose a more granular caching that does not include the config list and caches the timing for each config separately. Not sure if there's some subtlety I'm missing, but I don't think the other configs present in the autotuner should affect the timing for a given config.

Relevant function is:

https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/59c9ff171cd3adb5ca057cb40cfbf33bfb4c35ca/python/triton/runtime/autotuner.py#L170-L210
title: Feature request: cache autotune timing independent of config list

# Feature Request: Expose TTGIR Layout Attributes via Python API

## Summary

Add a Python-accessible API to retrieve the `#blocked` (and other) layout attributes assigned during TTGIR compilation, either as a field on `CompiledKernel.metadata` or via a dedicated method on the MLIR module bindings.

## Motivation

When performance-debugging Triton kernels, the **layout** assigned to tensors during the TTIR→TTGIR lowering pass is critical information. It determines:

- **Vectorization**: `sizePerThread` controls whether the compiler can emit `ld.global.v4.b32` (128-bit vectorized loads) vs scalar loads. A `sizePerThread=[4]` on a float32 tensor enables 4-wide vectorized access; `sizePerThread=[1]` forces scalar loads — a 4x bandwidth difference.

- **Thread-to-data mapping**: The combination of `sizePerThread`, `threadsPerWarp`, and `warpsPerCTA` determines exactly which elements each thread owns. This directly affects memory coalescing, bank conflicts in shared memory, and register pressure.

- **Number of groups per thread**: When `BLOCK_SIZE > sizePerThread × threadsPerWarp × warpsPerCTA`, each thread processes multiple "groups". Understanding this split (e.g., 1024 elements across 128 threads with sizePerThread=4 → 2 groups of 512) is essential for interpreting the generated PTX.

- **Dimension ordering**: The `order` field determines which dimension is contiguous in memory, affecting coalescing patterns in multi-dimensional kernels.

Currently, the **only** way to inspect these layout parameters is to parse the raw TTGIR text string from `compiled.asm['ttgir']`:

```
#blocked = #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread = [4], threadsPerWarp = [32], warpsPerCTA = [4], order = [0]}>
```

This requires regex parsing and is fragile. More importantly, the layout is decided inside the C++ compilation pipeline (by `add_convert_to_ttgpuir` and subsequent optimization passes like `add_coalesce`, `add_accelerate_matmul`), but the Python bindings for `ir.module` and `ir.type` do not expose layout information — `ir.type` only has `is_fp16()`, `is_integer()`, etc.

## Use Cases

1. **Performance debugging**: "Why is my kernel only hitting 60% memory bandwidth?" → Check if `sizePerThread` is too small for vectorized loads.

2. **Autotuning analysis**: Compare layouts across different `num_warps`/`BLOCK_SIZE` configurations to understand why one config is faster.

3. **Kernel development**: Verify the compiler assigned the expected layout after coalescing/optimization passes, without manually reading TTGIR dumps.

4. **Documentation/education**: Building tools that explain the compilation pipeline (e.g., annotated Python→TTIR→TTGIR→PTX comparisons) need structured layout data.

## Proposed API

### Option A: Add to `KernelMetadata` (minimal change)

Extract layouts from the TTGIR module text after `pm.run()` in the backend's `make_ttgir()` and store in the metadata dict:

```python
compiled = kernel[grid](...)
print(compiled.metadata.layouts)
# {'blocked': {'type': 'blocked', 'sizePerThread': [4], 'threadsPerWarp': [32], 'warpsPerCTA': [4], 'order': [0]}}
```

This approach works today with a small Python-side change (regex on `mod.str_nodebug()`), but is fragile — it depends on the MLIR text format.

### Option B: Add pybind11 binding (proper fix)

Expose a method on `ir.module` or `ir.type` that returns layout attributes as Python objects:

```python
# On the module level — all layout definitions used
mod.get_layouts()
# -> {'blocked': BlockedLayout(sizePerThread=[4], threadsPerWarp=[32], warpsPerCTA=[4], order=[0])}

# Or on individual values/types
val.get_type().get_layout()
# -> BlockedLayout(...)
```

This would require adding a C++ binding in `libtriton` that walks the MLIR module's encoding attributes and converts them to Python dicts or dataclasses. The `BlockedLayout` dataclass already exists in `triton.experimental.gluon.language._layouts` and could be reused.

## Workaround

We have implemented Option A locally as a proof-of-concept. The change is ~10 lines in `nvidia/compiler.py`'s `make_ttgir()`, parsing `#name = #ttg.type<{...}>` patterns from the TTGIR text after the pass manager runs. It works but depends on string format stability.

## Environment

- Triton version: 3.6.0
- Target: CUDA sm_100a (GB200)
title: Feature Request: Expose TTGIR layout attributes (sizePerThread, warpsPerCTA, etc.) via Python API

If there's only one config given to `@triton.autotune` it just deterministically returns that config, which makes sense: there's no point in autotuning if there's only one option. But if `prune_configs_by` returns only a single config, the autotuner still benchmarks it. I would propose that this should short-circuit for the same reason

https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/59c9ff171cd3adb5ca057cb40cfbf33bfb4c35ca/python/triton/runtime/autotuner.py#L215-L244

I think this just makes sense in general, but to elaborate a bit on the situation in which this has come up for me: I'm working with models (protein folding) where it is quite common for the input size to change basically every batch. This means that rather than being a one-time cost that is amortized across many batches, autotuning is additional overhead every batch (it's still amortized across many kernel calls within a batch, of course). The solution I'm playing with is to do aggressive config pruning if we're on known hardware where we can basically do offline autotuning and come up with heuristics for which config is best. In most cases, I'm trying to see if I can get it down to just a single configuration. The reasons I'm not using `@triton.heuristics` which conceptually seems like maybe a better match are: the API of a separate function per parameter is awkward for selecting entire configs, AFAICT it can't be used to select parameters like `num_warps` and `num_stages`, and I want to preserve the flexibility of being able to return multiple configs and have them picked via autotune both because sometimes the pattern of what config is best for a given range of input dimensions is so inscrutable that I don't think it can be captured in code, and because I think I want to preserve the ability for people to use autotuning if they want to, especially if running on hardware we haven't autotuned for.

The general situation is a more complicated, but I think the specific suggestion here is a simple fix that is in line with the existing behavior of autotune used with single-config lists.
title: Feature request: don't autotune if prune_configs_by returns a single config

Currently, triton_kernels is a separate package from Triton and is not published to PyPI. This makes it hard to consume by users, since they need to use one of the following workarounds:
1. Building Triton from source - for example, the approach in https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/main/examples/models/core/gpt_oss/README.md#using-openai-triton-kernels-for-moe
    - This approach requires additional work from users, including users of downstream / dependent libraries
3. Using HuggingFace's `kernels` package: https://huggingface.co/kernels-community/triton_kernels
    - This is pinned to a specific commit of `triton_kernels` and requires network access at runtime, which is not acceptable for many use cases
5. Installing `triton_kernels` directly from git via `pip install git+https://github.com/triton-lang/triton.git@main#subdirectory=python/triton_kernels`
    - This approach can cause issues with build systems and also slows down installation. 

Given the above, it would be great if `triton_kernels` was either (a) packaged within Triton, since the kernels depend on Triton anyway, or (b) published to PyPI as a separate package. This would improve UX for dependent libraries including TensorRT-LLM and `transformers`.

Related: the [`pyproject.toml`](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/main/python/triton_kernels/pyproject.toml) of `triton_kernels` needs updates - for example, `numpy` does not actually appear to be necessary, and `pytest` should be a dev dependency.
title: [triton_kernels][Feature Request] Publish triton_kernels to PyPI or package it alongside Triton

2:4 sparsity is supported on both AMD and NVIDIA GPUs and offers up to a 1.3x speedup over dense GEMMs. There’s been some previous work on doing this in a hardware-agnostic way in: https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/6714 

Sparsifying LLMs is an active area of research, often combined with quantization, and 2:4 sparse GEMM support in triton would make prototyping these kernels much easier.

On the modeling front, nearly every post-training sparsification technique reports accuracy on the 2:4 sparsity pattern, and there are some open-source 2:4 sparse [models](https://huggingface.co/RedHatAI/Sparse-Llama-3.1-8B-2of4) with 97% of the accuracy of their dense counterparts.

I'm confused about the implementation of matmul: [https://triton-lang.org/main/getting-started/tutorials/03-matrix-multiplication.html](https://triton-lang.org/main/getting-started/tutorials/03-matrix-multiplication.html)

```python
pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
num_pid_m = tl.cdiv(M, BLOCK_SIZE_M)
num_pid_n = tl.cdiv(N, BLOCK_SIZE_N)
num_pid_in_group = GROUP_SIZE_M * num_pid_n
group_id = pid // num_pid_in_group
first_pid_m = group_id * GROUP_SIZE_M
group_size_m = min(num_pid_m - first_pid_m, GROUP_SIZE_M)
pid_m = first_pid_m + (pid % group_size_m)  # problem here
pid_n = (pid % num_pid_in_group) // group_size_m
```
I think the following line
```python
pid_m = first_pid_m + (pid % group_size_m)
```
should be replaced by
```python
pid_m = first_pid_m + (pid % num_pid_in_group) % group_size_m
```

In most case (`group_size_m=GROUP_SIZE_M`), the two expressions will get same results, since `num_pid_in_group= GROUP_SIZE_M * num_pid_n`. But it's not the case when `group_size_m=num_pid_m - first_pid_m`.

- However, I have tried these two different implementations with different matrix sizes and found both of them work well.

- By the way, the tutorial states the triton implementation contains L2 cache optimizations, but I can't figure out how this happened in the implementation.
title: questions about matmul implementation

Triton is a parallel-execution language and pointer is a first-class type in triron.  So i have the following questions about it:

**1. What result triton expect when input pointer alias?**

Consider the following input(https://github.com/openai/triton/blob/main/python/tutorials/01-vector-add.py):
```
def add_kernel(
    x_ptr, 
    y_ptr,  
    output_ptr,
    n_elements, 
    BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr, 
):
    pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    block_start = pid * BLOCK_SIZE
    offsets = block_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = offsets < n_elements
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    output = x + y 
    tl.store(output_ptr + offsets, output, mask=mask)
```
If in runtime,  output_ptr is obtained by adding a small offset to x_ptr(e.g.: output_ptr = x_ptr + 64), does triton language expect kernel produce result same as output_ptr and x_ptr can never be alias?  Or input pointer alias is illegal in triton language?


**2. Does triton support pointer of pointer type?**
In mlir description, pointer of pointer type is something like  !tt.ptr<!tt.ptr<f16>>. This is a legal type in mlir, but takes difficulties to lowering it.

Any help would be appreciated, thanks.

_mean = tl.zeros([BLOCK_SIZE], dtype=tl.float32)
for off in range(0, N, BLOCK_SIZE):
    cols = off + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    a = tl.load(X + cols, mask=cols < N, other=0.).to(tl.float32)

But below, we enforce `N <= BLOCK_SIZE`:

body:
Hi Triton team,
Currently, tl.argmax provides a tie_break_left parameter. When set to True, it enforces strict leftmost semantics: in case of ties (multiple maximum values), it returns the smallest index.
However, when tie_break_left=False, the behavior is not symmetric: it does not guarantee rightmost semantics (i.e., returning the largest index among tied maxima). Instead, the tie-breaking behavior becomes non-deterministic or implementation-dependent, as seen in the current _argmax_combine reduction logic:
`@jit
def _argmax_combine(value1, index1, value2, index2, tie_break_left):
    if tie_break_left:
        tie = value1 == value2 and index1 < index2
    else:
        tie = False  # ← This means no tie-breaking; result depends on reduction order!
    gt = value1 > value2 or tie
    v_ret = core.where(gt, value1, value2)
    i_ret = core.where(gt, index1, index2)
    return v_ret, i_ret`
Because tie = False when tie_break_left=False, the comparison reduces to value1 > value2. In a parallel reduction tree, this means that which index "wins" among equal maxima depends on the traversal order, which is not guaranteed and may vary across runs or hardware.
This asymmetry makes it impossible to reliably implement rightmost argmax using the current API.
Proposal:
Introduce a way to enforce strict rightmost semantics. One option is to add a new parameter (e.g., tie_break_right) or reinterpret tie_break_left=False to mean "break ties to the right" (though this would be a breaking change). Alternatively, support an enum like tie='left' | 'right'.
For backward compatibility, perhaps keep the current tie_break_left but add a new argument, or allow tie_break_left=None for current behavior and False for rightmost.
Use case:
Rightmost argmax is useful in scenarios like finding the last occurrence of a maximum value (e.g., in sequence processing, attention masks, or debugging).
Thanks for considering!
title: Feature Request: Add strict rightmost semantics to tl.argmax when tie_break_left=False

### Describe the issue

## Issue

Hi, I'm implementing a matrix multiplication (X, R) × (R, Y) kernel in two different ways:

A 3D implementation, where XBLOCK, YBLOCK, and R0_BLOCK are exposed in three dimensions.
A 2D implementation, which maintains a 2D load pattern (similar to the Triton tutorial).

However, the 3D implementation is ~2× slower than the 2D one.
### Result
```
3D MM Time:
0.000856

2D MM Time:
0.000324
```

Given that the compiler should recognize that one of the dimensions in the 3D load is always 1, shouldn't both implementations have identical performance?


## Reproducible

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl

aten = torch.ops.aten
empty_strided_cuda = torch._C._dynamo.guards._empty_strided_cuda


@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config({"XBLOCK": 64, "YBLOCK": 64, "R0_BLOCK": 64}, num_stages=3, num_warps=8),
    ],
    key=[],
)
@triton.jit
def triton_3d_mm(in_ptr0, in_ptr1, out_ptr0, YBLOCK: tl.constexpr, XBLOCK: tl.constexpr, R0_BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    ynumel, xnumel, r0_numel = 2048, 2048, 2048
    RBLOCK: tl.constexpr = R0_BLOCK

    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    yoffset = tl.program_id(1) * YBLOCK
    roffset = 0

    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:, None, None]
    yindex = yoffset + tl.arange(0, YBLOCK)[None, :, None]
    r0_base = roffset + tl.arange(0, RBLOCK)[None, None, :]

    _tmp5 = tl.full([XBLOCK, YBLOCK], 0, tl.float32)
    for r0_offset in range(0, r0_numel, R0_BLOCK):
        r0_index = r0_offset + r0_base

        tmp0 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (r0_index + 2048 * yindex))  # (1,Y,R)
        tmp1 = tl.load(in_ptr1 + (xindex + 2048 * r0_index))  # (X,1,R)

        tmp0_ = tl.trans(tmp0.reshape([YBLOCK, RBLOCK]))  # (R,Y)
        tmp1_ = tmp1.reshape([XBLOCK, RBLOCK])  # (X,R)

        _tmp5 += tl.dot(tmp1_, tmp0_)  # (X,R) x (R,Y)

    _tmp5 = _tmp5[:,:,None] # (X,Y,1)
    tl.store(out_ptr0 + (xindex + 2048 * yindex), _tmp5.to(tl.float16))


@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config({"XBLOCK": 64, "YBLOCK": 64, "R0_BLOCK": 64}, num_stages=3, num_warps=8),
    ],
    key=[],
)
@triton.jit
def triton_2d_mm(in_ptr0, in_ptr1, out_ptr0, YBLOCK: tl.constexpr, XBLOCK: tl.constexpr, R0_BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    ynumel, xnumel, r0_numel = 2048, 2048, 2048
    RBLOCK: tl.constexpr = R0_BLOCK

    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    yoffset = tl.program_id(1) * YBLOCK
    roffset = 0

    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)
    yindex = yoffset + tl.arange(0, YBLOCK)
    r0_base = roffset + tl.arange(0, RBLOCK)

    _tmp5 = tl.full([XBLOCK, YBLOCK], 0, tl.float32)
    for r0_offset in range(0, r0_numel, R0_BLOCK):
        r0_index = r0_offset + r0_base

        tmp0 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (r0_index[:, None] + 2048 * yindex[None, :]))  # (R,Y)
        tmp1 = tl.load(in_ptr1 + (xindex[:, None] + 2048 * r0_index[None, :]))  # (X,R)

        _tmp5 += tl.dot(tmp1, tmp0)  # (X,R) x (R,Y)

    tl.store(out_ptr0 + (xindex[:, None] + 2048 * yindex[None, :]), _tmp5.to(tl.float16))  # (X,Y)


def call3d(args):
    arg0_1, arg1_1 = args
    torch.cuda.set_device(0)
    buf0 = empty_strided_cuda((2048, 2048), (2048, 1), torch.float16)
    grid = lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(2048, meta["XBLOCK"]), triton.cdiv(2048, meta["YBLOCK"]))
    triton_3d_mm[grid](arg0_1, arg1_1, buf0)
    return buf0,


def call2d(args):
    arg0_1, arg1_1 = args
    torch.cuda.set_device(0)
    buf0 = empty_strided_cuda((2048, 2048), (2048, 1), torch.float16)
    grid = lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(2048, meta["XBLOCK"]), triton.cdiv(2048, meta["YBLOCK"]))
    triton_2d_mm[grid](arg0_1, arg1_1, buf0)
    return buf0,


def benchmark_compiled_module(times=10, repeat=10):
    from torch._dynamo.testing import rand_strided
    from torch._inductor.utils import print_performance

    arg0_1 = rand_strided((2048, 2048), (2048, 1), device='cuda:0', dtype=torch.float16)
    arg1_1 = rand_strided((2048, 2048), (2048, 1), device='cuda:0', dtype=torch.float16)

    print("3D MM Time:")
    print_performance(lambda: call3d([arg0_1, arg1_1]), times=times, repeat=repeat)

    print("2D MM Time:")
    print_performance(lambda: call2d([arg0_1, arg1_1]), times=times, repeat=repeat)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    benchmark_compiled_module()
```

### Environment details

Triton: `main` branch (https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/commit/56a9adfbba6dc2f06b081d2a432c017c37086aaf)
GPU : RTX 3090

body:
### Summary

On an H100 (`sm90`), Triton crashes during compilation when `warp_specialize=True` is used on a simple pointer-based `tl.range` loop containing a `tl.dot`.

The failure happens in the `NVGPUWarpSpecialization` pass:

```text
/project/third_party/nvidia/hopper/lib/Transforms/WarpSpecialization/WSLowerToken.cpp:86:
void mlir::processProducerCommitOp(...): Assertion `false' failed.
...
Pipeline failed while executing [`NVGPUWarpSpecialization` on 'builtin.module' operation]
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed
```

This does **not** look like a generic `warp_specialize=True` failure on Hopper:
- a load-only loop compiles successfully with `warp_specialize=True`
- a descriptor-based single-loop attention-like kernel also compiles successfully with `warp_specialize=True`
- a small FA2-like causal two-loop descriptor kernel fails again

So the smallest trigger I found is: pointer-based loop + `tl.dot` + `warp_specialize=True` on Hopper.

This issue report and the reduced MWE were generated using Codex from a local reduction workflow.

### Environment

- Triton: `3.4.0`
- PyTorch: `2.8.0+cu128`
- Python: `3.11.13`
- GPU: `NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3`
- Compute capability: `sm90`
- NVIDIA driver: `580.126.09`
- Backend: `cuda`

### Minimal Repro

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def pointer_qk_only(
    q_ptr,
    k_ptr,
    o_ptr,
    N_CTX,
    HEAD_DIM: tl.constexpr,
    BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr,
    BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr,
    warp_specialize: tl.constexpr,
):
    start_m = tl.program_id(0)
    offs_m = start_m * BLOCK_M + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_M)
    offs_n = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N)
    offs_d = tl.arange(0, HEAD_DIM)

    q = tl.load(
        q_ptr + offs_m[:, None] * HEAD_DIM + offs_d[None, :],
        mask=(offs_m[:, None] < N_CTX),
        other=0.0,
    )
    last_qk = tl.zeros((BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N), dtype=tl.float32)

    for start_n in tl.range(0, N_CTX, BLOCK_N, warp_specialize=warp_specialize):
        start_n = tl.multiple_of(start_n, BLOCK_N)
        k = tl.load(
            k_ptr + (start_n + offs_n)[None, :] * HEAD_DIM + offs_d[:, None],
            mask=(start_n + offs_n)[None, :] < N_CTX,
            other=0.0,
        )
        last_qk = tl.dot(q, k)

    tl.store(
        o_ptr + offs_m[:, None] * BLOCK_N + offs_n[None, :],
        last_qk,
        mask=(offs_m[:, None] < N_CTX) & (offs_n[None, :] < BLOCK_N),
    )


def run(flag: bool):
    n_ctx = 128
    head_dim = 64
    block_m = 64
    block_n = 32
    q = torch.randn((n_ctx, head_dim), device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
    k = torch.randn((n_ctx, head_dim), device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
    o = torch.empty((n_ctx, block_n), device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
    grid = (triton.cdiv(n_ctx, block_m),)
    pointer_qk_only[grid](
        q,
        k,
        o,
        n_ctx,
        HEAD_DIM=head_dim,
        BLOCK_M=block_m,
        BLOCK_N=block_n,
        warp_specialize=flag,
        num_warps=4,
        num_stages=2,
    )
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print(f"warp_specialize={flag} PASS")


run(False)  # passes
run(True)   # fails in NVGPUWarpSpecialization on H100
```

### Observed Behavior

- `warp_specialize=False`: compiles and runs
- `warp_specialize=True`: fails during compilation in `NVGPUWarpSpecialization`

### Additional Reduction Notes

I also checked a few nearby cases locally:

- `pointer_load_only` with `warp_specialize=True`: passes
- pointer-based `tl.dot(p, v, acc)` loop with `warp_specialize=True`: fails
- descriptor-based single-loop attention-like kernel with `warp_specialize=True`: passes
- descriptor-based FA2-like causal two-loop kernel with `warp_specialize=True`: fails

That makes me suspect the Hopper warp-specialization lowering has a bug around some pointer-based producer/consumer token pattern for loop-carried `tl.dot`, and that a more FA2-like two-loop structure can also trigger it even on descriptor paths.

### Reproducer Output

```text
python: /project/third_party/nvidia/hopper/lib/Transforms/WarpSpecialization/WSLowerToken.cpp:86: void mlir::processProducerCommitOp(OpBuilder &, ttnvws::ProducerCommitOp, Value, ttnvws::TokenLoadType, unsigned int): Assertion `false' failed.
...
Pipeline failed while executing [`NVGPUWarpSpecialization` on 'builtin.module' operation]
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed
```
title: [Hopper] NVGPUWarpSpecialization crashes on simple pointer-based tl.dot loop with warp_specialize=True

## Description
Refactor the `createConstantI32` helper function in `lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/Utility.cpp` to use `mlir::ImplicitLocOpBuilder`. 

Currently, many conversion patterns and utility functions manually pass both `mlir::Location` and `mlir::OpBuilder`. This introduces redundant boilerplate and increases the risk of passing an inconsistent `Location` context during complex IR generation.

## Proposed Changes
To ensure a smooth transition and avoid breaking all call sites simultaneously, I propose a **two-step refactoring approach** using C++ function overloading:

### 1. Introduce the New Signature
Add the refactored version in `Utility.h` and `Utility.cpp` that accepts the implicit builder:
```cpp
Value createConstantI32(ImplicitLocOpBuilder &b, int32_t v);
```
### 2. Maintain Legacy Support (Overloading)
Keep the original signature as a temporary wrapper to facilitate incremental migration:
```cpp
// Legacy wrapper to be deprecated
inline Value createConstantI32(Location loc, OpBuilder &rewriter, int32_t v) {
  ImplicitLocOpBuilder b(loc, rewriter);
  return createConstantI32(b, v);
}
```

### 3. Incremental Migration
Update call sites throughout``` lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/``` to use the new ```ImplicitLocOpBuilder``` context. Once all call sites are updated, the legacy version will be removed.

## Motivation
-  Reduce Boilerplate: Eliminates repetitive loc arguments in high-density IR generation files (e.g., DotOpToLLVM.cpp, ElementwiseOpToLLVM.cpp).
- Alignment with MLIR Best Practices: Modernizes the codebase to follow the recommended builder patterns in MLIR.
- Risk Management: Overloading allows for safer, smaller PRs and easier code reviews.

## Validation
- [ ] Build Triton from source.
- [ ] Verify with ninja check-triton to ensure no functional regressions in the generated IR.

## Plan
I intend to start with a targeted cleanup of createConstantI32. By C++ function overloading to keep the legacy signature as a wrapper, the new API to be available without requiring an immediate update to all call sites. 

If the maintainers agree with this direction, I am happy to submit a PR and potentially expand this to other similar constants/helpers in Utility.cpp in future tasks.

Does this refactor align with the current development roadmap for Triton's backend? I would appreciate your feedback before I proceed with the implementation.
title: Migrate `createConstantI32` to `ImplicitLocOpBuilder` in `Utility.cpp`

whenever I try just following the instructions. After debugging, I noticed that there is no `2.1.0` version available in the [Releases](https://github.com/openai/triton/tags)  or the [PyPI page](https://pypi.org/project/triton/#history).

I was able to fix this issue when I changed the following lines in `setup.py`:

```python
....
 setup(
     name="triton",
     version="2.1.0",
     author="Philippe Tillet",
     author_email="phil@openai.com",
....
```
To:
```python
...
 setup(
     name="triton",
     version="2.0.0",
     author="Philippe Tillet",
     author_email="phil@openai.com",
...
```

The installation now succeeds:
```bash
Installing collected packages: triton
  Attempting uninstall: triton
    Found existing installation: triton 2.0.0
    Uninstalling triton-2.0.0:
      Successfully uninstalled triton-2.0.0
  Running setup.py develop for triton
Successfully installed triton
```

I can submit a PR if this seems like a real issue. I apologize if it isn't.

Thanks!

body:
### 📚 The doc issue

Hi,


[Default `torch.compile` + backward behavior under autocast is documented as:](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/user_guide/torch_compiler/torch.compiler_backward.html#autocast-behavior):

> "same_as_forward" (default). We assume that the backward of the torch.compile’ed region will be run under the same autocast context manager that the region was run under (if any).

However, [the `torch.amp` docs themselves explicitly call out](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/amp.html):

> [autocast](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/amp.html#torch.autocast) should wrap only the forward pass(es) of your network, including the loss computation(s). Backward passes under autocast are not recommended. Backward ops run in the same type that autocast used for corresponding forward ops.

This is extremely misleading. If the recommended practice is *not* to perform backward under autocast, why is the default assumption that backward is performed under autocast if autocast is enabled in the forward?

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Short of changing the default (which would be a breaking change, so obviously not a light thing to do), call out the discrepancy loudly around both docs. This deserves a serious warning IMO since it can have deep numerical correctness implications, and affects all backward-pass computations.

### 📚 The doc issue

requesting to add `FlopCounterMode` documentation

and to include the following notes from these discussion:

1. https://pytorch.slack.com/archives/C3PDTEV8E/p1712785539175899 (elementwise ops aren't counted - and why)
2. https://pytorch.slack.com/archives/C3PDTEV8E/p1712798211869749?thread_ts=1712786199.970369&cid=C3PDTEV8E  torch.compile usage: the intended usage is to use it on an uncompiled version of the model first.

4. the mode counts only matmul, conv, attn - may be a few other high intense blocks, but it doesn't count almost anything else (not `sin`, `mul`, any element-wise ops). Perhaps  the best advice to add here would be to use `FlopCounterMode(display=True)` while debugging since it gives the exact breakdown of which ops it measured - which means everything else is ignored.
5. document that it will not count custom kernels and how to make it count those (register FLOP formulas for them)
3. let's perhaps include the very cool integration Lightning folks (Carlos Mocholi et al) did using the meta-model: https://pytorch.slack.com/archives/C3PDTEV8E/p1712788665140289?thread_ts=1712786199.970369&cid=C3PDTEV8E - may be this could be a util provided by pytorch? (edit: when tried this is practice - apparently this meta device solution will often fail if an op isn't implemented on meta.)

-----

**mar-2025 update**: Additionally the user needs to be aware that running `FlopCounterMode` incurs a significant overhead in both compute and memory usage - which renders it unusable in many use cases where gpu memory is tight. Compute isn't a problem if the result is cached, but memory usage overhead leads to OOM when `FlopCounterMode` is run and the memory was close to being full.

body:
Guys,
This probably isn't my business, but I want to point out that you are building up technical debt by not putting effort into internal documentation at the C++ level.  Class Reducer, for example, doesn't have good documentation either from the higher-level or the detailed level; and this isn't the kind of code where you can credibly claim that it's self-documenting.

By higher-level I mean a many-paragraph comment block describing what is the basic design approach: a description of the algorithm that's being implemented, with special cases and so on stripped out, to give a high-level understanding, then what are some details of the design that might not be obvious, what are the pitfalls, and so on, starting from the more important to the less important.

By detailed level I mean documentation of the individual functions: what does the function do, what are the individual arguments (their format and purpose, and preconditions they must satisfy), what does the function return, when is it called, and so on.  Only maybe 10% of this is done.  For example, in the comment for the constructor, only one of the 10 arguments is mentioned by name, and the name is wrong.

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/38c185189c4e7b11f9bd9b60afed75b367ee00e2/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/reducer.hpp#L109

I get it, move fast and break things, and PyTorch is great of course, but I feel like you'd get a lot of benefit from a little work here, and you'd even save time within your own team and be less f*cked if one of your key guys gets a deadly virus or something.

body:
### New Feature for Release

It would potentially be great to have a polar decomposition implemented in PyTorch.
Polar decomposition is useful in applications like Graphics, Vision, Quantum Computing, among others.
It can be used as an alternative to the Newton-Schulz step in the popular Muon optimizer (https://kellerjordan.github.io/posts/muon/). In general, it is a useful tool for orthogonalization.

cuSOLVER is to offer an implementation of the QR-based Dynamically Weighted Halley (QDWH) algorithm (proposed in https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/090774999, but adapted for HPC).
JAX exposes the algorithm directly, see https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/_autosummary/jax.lax.linalg.qdwh.html and https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/blob/main/jax/_src/tpu/linalg/qdwh.py#L121 (I assume it follows https://www.netlib.org/utk/people/JackDongarra/PAPERS/task-polor-sc23.pdf).

The algorithm can expose the SVD decomposition (see https://epubs.siam.org/doi/abs/10.1137/120876605). Conversely, the SVD can be used to derive the polar decomposition, but that inflicts a significant performance cost (in complexity and memory).

The decomposition is not hard to implement the JVP/VJP rules for, so it can be brought to the same level of integration as other `torch.linalg` operations.

body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Motivated by:
- https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/158698

It's sometimes useful in eager non-differentiable code to be able to downcast inplace (float32->bfloat16 for reduce_dtype->param_dtype, float32->int16 for pcm audio conversions; but also bfloat16<>float16, int16<>bfloat16) to avoid another big memory allocation (but when we know for sure that this tensor will get deallocated soon anyway, so we're okay that half-storage is lying around unused for now)

A basic prototype from:
- https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/158698#issuecomment-3092481798

seems working (but might be a more reliable / speedy version without constantly calling clone() is possible, or maybe somehow cloning into a buffer to ensure a single, constant buffer allocation):
```python
import torch

def to_(tensor1d, dtype, *, split_size = 1024):
    assert tensor1d.ndim == 1
    assert tensor1d.dtype.itemsize % dtype.itemsize == 0
    k, dst = 0, tensor1d.view(dtype)
    for chunk in tensor1d.split(split_size):
        dst[k : k + len(chunk)] = chunk.clone() # RuntimeError: unsupported operation: some elements of the input tensor and the written-to tensor refer to a single memory location. Please clone() the tensor before performing the operation.
        k += len(chunk)
    return dst[:k]

if __name__ == '__main__':
    a = torch.ones(4, dtype = torch.float32)
    print(a, a.dtype, a.dtype.itemsize, a.nbytes)

    b = to_(a, torch.bfloat16)
    print(b, b.dtype, b.dtype.itemsize, b.nbytes)
```

---

Or might be better to model this as `torch.to_`:
- https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/69431

body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## Problem Statement
When implementing reinforcement learning algorithms like SAC, we need efficient experience replay buffers to store and sample transitions (state, action, reward, next_state). Currently, many implementations resort to custom circular arrays instead of using Python's built-in data structures like `collections.deque`. This is because, as noted in [[ManiSkill issue #881](https://github.com/haosulab/ManiSkill/issues/881)](https://github.com/haosulab/ManiSkill/issues/881), storing CUDA tensors in Python's deque is inefficient as it's designed primarily for CPU objects and Python primitives.

## Feature Request
I propose adding a CUDA-optimized queue/circular buffer data structure to PyTorch that efficiently handles tensor operations, particularly for CUDA tensors. This would provide native support for queue operations that maintain GPU residency throughout.

## Potential Implementation
The implementation could:
- Leverage CUDA memory management for efficient storage
- Possibly use `torch.roll` or similar operations for efficient circular behavior
- Provide standard queue operations (enqueue, dequeue, sample) optimized for tensors
- Support batched operations common in deep learning workflows
- Include options for fixed size buffers (important for replay memory)

## Benefits
1. **Performance**: Eliminate CPU-GPU transfers when managing sequential data
2. **Simplicity**: Reduce boilerplate code in RL implementations
3. **Standardization**: Provide an optimized, tested solution instead of custom implementations
4. **Broader applications**: Useful beyond RL for sequential modeling, online learning, etc.

## Use Cases
- Replay buffers in reinforcement learning
- Sequence modeling with sliding windows
- Online learning algorithms
- Any application requiring FIFO operations on GPU tensors

I'm a student studying machine learning, and I noticed this gap while analyzing RL codebases. I believe this addition would benefit many PyTorch users working with sequential data on GPUs.

body:
### Feature request: `DataLoader` using multithreading instead of multiprocessing

A version of `DataLoader` that uses **multithreading** would bring several advantages:

* Lower inter-process communication and pickling overhead; in some cases this is much faster. See the blogpost by Nvidia showcasing it: https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/improved-data-loading-with-threads/
* Dramatically lower memory usage because threads share address space.
* No need to pick between `fork`, `forkserver`, or `spawn` start methods and choosing the disadvantages of one of these.

Multiprocessing is mainly used to bypass the GIL, but that argument is weakening:

* Many data-loading steps (network I/O, Image decode, decompression) release the GIL anyway, so multiple threads can overlap them.
* Starting with Python 3.13 the GIL can be disabled entirely, further reducing the benefit of processes. 

### Suggested interface

```python
DataLoader(
    dataset,
    num_workers=8,
    worker_backend="thread",   # default stays "process"
)
```

body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

A sparse tensor can be viewed as a pair of indices and values that define the set of specified tensor elements. PyTorch supports sparse tensors with COO and CSR formats and starting from https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/75831, also CSC, BSR, and BSC formats.

All mentioned sparse formats use the `.values()` method to retrieve the values of specified sparse tensor elements. However, the API for accessing the indices of sparse tensor elements lacks uniformity and completeness:
- the indices of COO tensors are provided via the `.indices()` method
- the indices of CSR and BSR tensors are provided via the `.crow_indices()` and `.col_indices()` methods
- the indices of CSC and BSC tensors can be accessed via the `.crow_indices()` and `.col_indices()` methods as a temporary defect. It is a defect because `crow_indices()` returns the compressed column indices and `col_indices()` returns the row indices.

The motivation for creating this issue is
1. to resolve the temporary defect of accessing the indices of CSC and BSC tensors
2. to design a more uniform API for accessing sparse tensor indices of any sparse format

In the following, a number of possible solutions will be outlined for discussion.

## ~Proposal 1~ A fix to the CSC/BSC defect.

To address the reported defect of CSC and BSC tensors, a natural extension to the current convention of accessing indices is to introduce new methods `.ccol_indices()` and `.row_indices()` that will return the compressed row indices and column indices, respectively.

In addition, the methods `.crow_indices()` and `.col_indices()` will be supported only for sparse CSR and BSR tensors. The methods `.ccol_indices()` and `.row_indices()` will be supported only for sparse CSC and BSC tensors.

This option is actionable per https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/76638#issuecomment-1115405207

## :+1: Proposal 2

To reduce the number of indices related methods within the class of compressed tensors (CSR, CSC, BSR, BSC), another option is to introduce new methods `.compressed_indices()` and `.plain_indices()` that will return compressed row indices and column indices, respectively, for CSR and BSR tensors, and compressed column indices and row indices for CSC and BSC tensors.

In addition, the methods `.crow_indices()` and `.col_indices()` would be deprecated.

## :tada: Proposal 3

To reduce the number of the related methods even more and to unify the API in between all sparse formats, the third option is to reuse the existing `.indices()` method for retrieving the indices data for all compressed tensors, that is, for CSR and BSR tensors, it would return a 2-tuple that first item contains compressed row indices and the second item contains column indices. Similar, for CSC and BSR tensors, the `.indices()` would return a tuple of compressed column indices and row indices.

In addition, the methods `.crow_indices()` and `.col_indices()` would be deprecated.

In general, for any new sparse tensor format, the `.indices()` would return an object that contains indices data in a form that is most natural for the given format.

## :rocket: Proposal 4

From https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/76638#issuecomment-1115398434: Introduce optional `dim` option to `.indices()` method so that
- for COO tensors, we would have `coo.indices(dim=d) == coo.indices()[d]`
- for CSR/... tensors, `csr.indices(dim=d) == (csr.crow_indices() if d == 0 else csr.col_indices())`
- as a possible extension, for strided tensors, `dense.indices(dim=...)` returns indices tensor equivalent to `dense.to_sparse_coo().indices(dim=...)`.

## :smile: Proposal 5

From https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/76638#issuecomment-1115398434: Introduce `Indices` data structure such that
- for COO tensors, `.indices()` has the current behaviour, that is, return a tensor of indices
- for CSR/... tensors, `csr.indices()` returns `Indices` instance such that `torch.tensor(csr.indices()) == csr.to_sparse_coo().indices()` but internally, the row indices are compressed within the `Indices` object.

### Alternatives

An alternative is to copy the sparse tensor indices API from `scipy.sparse` where [sparse CSR tensor indices](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.sparse.csr_matrix.html), for instance, can be accessed via attributes `.indptr` and `.indices` that correspond to compressed row indices and column indices, respectively. Clearly, the `scipy.sparse` API is incompatible with the corresponding API in PyTorch (e.g. compare `indices` being a column indices specific attribute in SciPy vs being an all-dimensions indices specific method in PyTorch).


### Additional context

_No response_

body:
# Introduction

As machine learning models continue to grow in size (ex: OpenAI GPT-2 with 1.5B parameters, OpenAI GPT-3 with 175B parameters), traditional [Distributed DataParallel](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/ddp.html) (DDP) training no longer scales as these models don’t fit on a single GPU device. As a result, we need to leverage some sort of model parallelism techniques to train such large models. There are several techniques in the industry that have been employed to achieve this goal. Some examples include [GShard](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16668) and [Mesh-Tensorflow](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.02084) from Google,  [ZeRO](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054) from Microsoft and [Megatron-LM](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.08053) from Nvidia.

Although, one of the first approach to attempt to solve this problem was pipeline parallelism as described in the [GPipe](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1811.06965.pdf) paper. The high level idea is to partition the layers of a model sequentially across several GPUs and then split a mini-batch of data into multiple micro-batches and execute these micro-batches in a pipelined fashion across multiple devices. 

This idea is illustrated in Figure 1 below where a mini-batch is split into 4 micro-batches and its execution is pipelined across 4 GPUs. **Fi,j** denotes the forward pass for micro-batch **j** on GPU **i** and **Bi,j** denotes the backward pass for micro-batch **j** on GPU **i**. The update in the end is the optimizer that applies all the gradients.

![Screen Shot 2020-08-02 at 4 53 18 PM](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9958665/93392490-b907dc80-f825-11ea-9dd5-00ff3e08de37.png)
                                                                           **Figure 1 (GPipe)**

PyTorch currently provides the basic primitives for users to build such pipelined training themselves. Although as we shall see below, pipeline parallelism involves quite a bit of complexity and it would be extremely useful for users if we could provide an easy to use framework (like DDP) for them. In addition to this pipeline parallelism has been widely studied and used for training large models and as a result it makes it a perfect starting point for PyTorch to support training large models.

# Related Work

Pipeline parallelism is an active research area with several different approaches to the problem. [torchgpipe](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.09910) is an implementation of GPipe in PyTorch and goes into the nitty gritty details of how to implement such a framework in PyTorch. The [fairscale](https://github.com/facebookresearch/fairscale) project has [forked](https://github.com/facebookresearch/fairscale/tree/master/fairscale/nn/pipe) torchgpipe to provide an implementation of GPipe for various research teams in FAIR.

As you can see in Figure 1, GPipe has some challenges in effectively utilizing GPU resources since it has a pipeline bubble due to the synchronous nature of training. The “update” step at the end needs to synchronize all GPUs and update the parameters before moving onto the next micro-batch. An alternative to this is an asynchronous pipelining approach that is adopted by [PipeDream](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.03377.pdf) (Figure 2) and [XPipe](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.04610). 

As you can see in Figure 2, a mini-batch is split into 4 micro-batches, but the pipeline admits micro-batches from the next mini-batch before the current mini-batch has completely finished. The first mini-batch consists of (1, 2, 3, 4) as micro-batches and the next mini-batch consists of (5, 6, 7, 8). But device 1 starts executing micro-batch 5 as soon as micro-batch 1 is done. This approach provides better GPU utilization and as a result better training throughput, although it also introduces some parameter staleness that can reduce training accuracy.

![Screen Shot 2020-08-02 at 5 16 59 PM](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9958665/93392994-8f9b8080-f826-11ea-98ed-ef9dad5875fc.png)
**Figure 2 (PipeDream)**

As a result, pipelining approaches can be divided into two broad categories:

1. **Synchronous (GPipe/torchgpipe)**: GPUs are not fully utilized in this approach, although it provides better training accuracy and doesn’t affect the existing training loop much. In addition to this, memory utilization is low since we only keep a single version of the weights.
2. **Asynchronous (PipeDream/XPipe)**: GPU utilization is much better compared to Synchronous and results in better training throughput. Although, parameter staleness could affect model quality and the asynchronous nature needs some modifications to continuously feed data into the system. In order to overcome the parameter staleness issue, the asynchronous systems usually store multiple versions of the weights (weight stashing/weight prediction) resulting in increased memory utilization. 

# Target Use Cases

The use case here is mostly for large NLP/CV models that don't fit on a single GPU and this is what Gpipe, torchgpipe, PipeDream and XPipe target. For these use cases, it might be beneficial to provide users the flexibility to choose from synchronous and asynchronous pipelining approaches based on the tradeoffs they are comfortable with.

# API Proposal

The high level idea is to support two different APIs  for synchronous and asynchronous pipeline parallelism. The reason for two different APIs is due to the fact that the way these APIs would be used would be very different from each other.


## torch.distributed.pipeline_async (Option1)

```
torch.distributed.PipelineAsyncModel(
    pipeline: nn.Sequential,
    per_stage_optim: List[OptimSpec],
    chunks: int = 1)
 
class OptimSpec {
  optimizer_class # Subclass of torch.optim.Optimizer (https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/optim.html#torch.optim.Optimizer).
  module_to_optimize # The nn.Module (could be RemoteModule) that needs to be 
                       optimized.
  optimizer_args # args to build the optimizer instance.
  optimizer_kwargs # kwargs to build the optimizer instance.
}
    
Arguments:

pipeline: nn.Sequential (https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.Sequential.html) where each nn.Module in the list is placed on the 
          appropriate device(CPU or GPU)/machine by the user. Note that the 
          nn.Sequential could also consist of RemoteModule (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/distributed/nn/api/remote_module.py#L147) for cross host 
          pipelining.
per_stage_optim: List of OptimSpec, one for each stage of the pipeline. 
                 Should have exactly the same number of elements as pipeline. We use 
                 an OptimSpec here instead of a list of actual optimizer instances 
                 since we don't want to create all the optimizer instances locally. 
                 Instead, we'd like to get a spec and the pipeline can create the 
                 optimizers for the appropriate stages on the appropriate 
                 hosts/devices.
chunks: Number of micro-batches.

    
PipelineAsyncModel Interface:

    PipelineAsyncModel is an interface and users need to override this class to create 
    an appropriate pipeline instance. The PipelineAsyncModel provides a handful of 
    methods and the rest need to be implemented by the user. The methods mentioned as 
    "interface" below have to be implemented by the user.
    
    PipelineAsyncModel.forward(self, *args, **kwargs) -> MinibatchProcessor
        Runs the forward pass for the model asynchronously and returns a 
        "MinibatchProcessor" handle.
        
    PipelineAsyncModel.forward_pre_hook(
        microbatch_input,
        stage_idx,
        microbatch_idx) -> None
        
        Called before the forward pass is called on any stage/microbatch in the pipeline.
        Can be used to perform weight prediction. 
   
    # interface method
    PipelineAsyncModel.forward_post_hook_final_stage(
            microbatch_output: Tensor, 
            microbatch_idx: int
            target: Tensor = None, # Tensor/Parameter/ParameterList/nn.Module (anything that supports .to())
            dist_autograd_context_id: int,
            ) -> None 
            
        The "forward_post_hook" method is called for every microbatch on the last stage 
        when the forward pass for the microbatch is complete. The purpose of the 
        "forward_post_hook" is to compute the loss for the microbatch once it is done 
        and initiate the backward pass. 
        "forward_post_hook" has to be pickleable.
            
        Arguments:
            microbatch_output: Output of the forward pass of the microbatch.
            microbatch_idx: Index of the microbatch that we are processing.
            target: Usually the "target" Tensor that would be used to compute the 
                    loss, the pipeline automatically moves the "target" to the last 
                    stage in the pipeline and on the appropriate device as well.
            dist_autograd_context_id: The distributed autograd context id to use for 
                                      the backward pass. If None, local autograd can be 
                                      used.
   
    # interface method
    PipelineAsyncModel.backward_post_hook(
            per_stage_optim: torch.optim.Optimizer, 
            microbatch_idx: int,
            stage_idx: int) -> None
            
        The "backward_post_hook" method is invoked once the backward pass of a particular 
        microbatch has finished on a particular stage. The purpose of this callback
        is to perform the appropriate optimizer operations (zero_grads, step etc.)
                    
        Arguments:
             per_stage_optim: The optimizer for this stage, which is built based on 
                              the OptimSpec provided for this stage.
             microbatch_idx: Index of the microbatch that we are processing.
             stage_idx: Index of the stage on which we are running.
   
    PipelineAsyncModel.save_current_stage(key:str, value: object) -> None
        
        Saves a key:value pair on the current stage of the pipeline. This can only be 
        used in the provided hooks (forward_post_hook, backward_post_hook etc.) to save 
        data on the appropriate stage of the pipeline. This can be used for weight 
        stashing/prediction.
        
    PipelineAsyncModel.save_on_stage(key:str, value: object, stage_id, device_id) -> None
        
        Saves a key:value pair on the given stage of the pipeline. This can be used to 
        save any additional state on a particular stage and retrieve it accordingly. 
        Using the device_id option, this state can be saved on either CPU or GPU.
        
    PipelineAsyncModel.retrieve_current_stage(key:str) -> object
    
        Retrieve the value on the current stage that was stored using 
        "save_current_stage"
        
    PipelineAsyncModel.module_for_current_stage() -> torch.nn.Module
    
        This can only be used in the provided hooks (forward_post_hook, 
        backward_post_hook etc.) to to get the nn.Module for the current stage.
   
    MinibatchProcessor.set_target(target: Tensor) -> None
        Sets the "target" for the minibatch we are processing. This "target" 
        is moved to the appropriate device on the last stage of the pipeline 
        and is passed to the "forward_post_hook".

Examples:

# This is an example of a pipeline across two machines each using one GPU.
# On worker 0
layer1 = nn.Linear(10, 5).cuda(0)
# Need to enhance RemoteModule to include device for this purposes.
layer2 = RemoteModule("worker1", device="cuda:0", nn.Linear, 5, 1) 

pipeline = nn.Sequential(layer1, layer2)

# Build the optim_spec
optim_spec1 = OptimSpec(optim.SGD, layer1, lr=0.05)
optim_spec2 = OptimSpec(optim.SGD, layer2, lr=0.05)

class SimplePipelineModel(torch.distributed.PipelineAsyncModel):

    def forward_post_hook(microbatch_output, microbatch_idx, target, context_id):
        loss = F.cross_entropy(microbatch_output, target[microbatch_idx])
        dist_autograd.backward([loss], context_id)

    def backward_post_hook(per_stage_optim, microbatch_idx, stage_idx):
        per_stage_optim.step()
        per_stage_optim.zero_grads()    

model = torch.distributed.SimplePipelineModel(
            pipeline, 
            [optim_spec1, optim_spec2], 
            chunks = 4)

for minibatch, target in data:
     model(minibatch).set_target(target)
```

## torch.distributed.pipeline_async (Option2)

```
torch.distributed.pipeline_async(
    data_iter: Iterator,
    pipeline: nn.Sequential,
    dist_optim: DistributedOptimizer,    
    loss_func: Callable,
    chunks: int = 1) -> PipelineAsyncModel
    
Arguments:

data_iter: An iterator to data consisting of a tuple of input data and the 
           associated target for that data.
pipeline: nn.Sequential (https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.Sequential.html) where each nn.Module in the list is placed on the 
          appropriate device(CPU or GPU)/machine by the user. Note that the 
          nn.Sequential could also consist of RemoteModule (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/distributed/nn/api/remote_module.py#L147) for cross host 
          pipelining.
dist_optim: An instance of DistributedOptimizer (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/distributed/optim/optimizer.py#L58) to optimize the relevant 
            parameters of the model. Note that we need to use 
            DistributedOptimizer here since we could have pipelining across
            hosts. By default, the optimizer is run inline once the 
            backward pass completes for a parameter.
loss_func: A Callable that will be passed the output and target for each 
           microbatch in the pipeline and it is responsible to return the loss 
           based on that. The returned loss will be used to run the backward 
           pass.
chunks: Number of micro-batches.

Example:

# This is an example of a pipeline across two machines each using one GPU.
# On worker 0
data = [
    (torch.rand(10, 10), torch.rand(10, 1), 
    (torch.rand(5, 10), torch.rand(5, 1), 
]

layer1 = nn.Linear(10, 5).cuda(0)

# Need to enhance RemoteModule to include device for this purposes.
layer2 = RemoteModule("worker1", device="cuda:0", nn.Linear, 5, 1) 
pipeline = nn.Sequential(layer1, layer2)

rref_params = [RRef(param) for param in layer1.parameters()]
# Need to enhance RemoteModule for `get_rref_parameters`
rref_params.append(layer2.get_rref_parameters())

dist_optim = DistributedOptimizer(optim.SGD, rref_params, lr=0.05)

# Loss function for the pipeline.
def loss_func(microbatch_output, microbatch_target):
    return F.cross_entropy(microbatch_output, microbatch_target)

# Now run the pipeline on our data.
torch.distributed.pipeline_async(
    iter(data), 
    pipeline, 
    dist_optim,
    loss_func,
    chunks = 4)
```

**Note on DDP:** Given the async nature of the pipeline, we can’t wrap this pipeline easily in DDP since there really is no synchronization point in the pipeline where we can decide to have DDP to start allreducing the gradients. In addition to this, DDP would kind of allreduce after each minibatch which defeats the point of an async pipeline and makes it more inline with the synchronous counter part. Although, if we’d like to run pipeline_async for a model across multiple GPUs in a single host, but Distributed DataParallel across replicas of the model across multiple hosts, we can introduce a parameter called sync_every_minibatches which basically adds a synchronization point after sync_every_minibatches is done and synchronizes all model parameters across different hosts.

## torch.distributed.pipeline_async (Option3)

```
model = torch.distributed.pipeline_async(
            pipeline, 
            [optim_spec1, optim_spec2], 
            chunks = 4)
            
futures = []
for microbatch, target in data:
    futures.append(
        # this returns a special Future that contains the autograd context id
        model(microbatch)  
            # this will forward it's autograd context id to chained future
            # and the then function all be wrapped with that context
            .then(lambda out_future: loss_fn(target, out_future.wait()))  
            # the future.then wrapps the returned tensor with custom tensor 
            # type that overrides the backward function which calls dist.backward
            .then(lambda loss_future: loss.backward())  
    )
        
 torch.futures.collect_all(futures).then(lambda unused: optimizer.step())

Different stages can be chained using .then. If we still get complains that the above API is different from today’s PyTorch API, I guess we can offer loss function and optimizer wrappers that internally calls the .then API.

loss_fn = AsyncLossFn(F.cross_entropy)
opt = AsyncOptimizer(DistributedOptimizer(optim.SGD, rref_params, lr=0.05))

for minibatch, target in data:
    out_future = model(minibatch)
    loss_future = loss_fn(out_future, target)
    bwd_future = loss_future.backward()
    opt.wait_for(bwd_future)
    
opt_done_future = opt.step()
```

## torch.distributed.pipeline_sync

```
# Note: This API is very similar to torchgpipe and inspired from it.
# torchgpipe API for reference: https://torchgpipe.readthedocs.io/en/stable/api.html

torch.distributed.pipeline_sync(
    pipeline: nn.Sequential,
    checkpoint: CheckpointEnum = EXCEPT_LAST, # ALWAYS, EXCEPT_LAST, NEVER 
    chunks: int = 1) -> PipelineSyncModel

Arguments:

pipeline: nn.Sequential (https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.Sequential.html) where each nn.Module in the list is placed on the 
          appropriate device(CPU or GPU)/machine by the user. Note that 
          nn.Sequential could also consist of RemoteModule (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/distributed/nn/api/remote_module.py#L147) for cross host 
          pipelining.
checkpoint: Enum that determines which checkpointing mode to use.
chunks: Number of micro-batches.

Returns:
    An instance of PipelineSyncModel

Forward Method

PipelineSyncModel.forward(self, *input, **kwargs) -> RRef

Returns:
    RRef to output corresponding to the result of the minibatch. 
    Since we plan to support cross host pipelining, the RRef could be on a 
    device on a different host.
    
Example:

# This is an example of a pipeline across two machines each using one GPU.
# On worker 0
layer1 = nn.Linear(10, 5).cuda(0)
# Need to enhance RemoteModule to include device for this purposes.
layer2 = RemoteModule("worker1", device="cuda:0", nn.Linear, 5, 1) 

pipeline = nn.Sequential(layer1, layer2)
model = torch.distributed.pipeline_sync(pipeline, chunks = 4)

rref_params = [RRef(param) for param in layer1.parameters()]
# Need to enhance RemoteModule for `get_rref_parameters`
rref_params.append(layer2.get_rref_parameters())

dist_optim = DistributedOptimizer(optim.SGD, rref_params, lr=0.05)

# Helper functions
def compute_loss(output_rref, target_rref):
    return F.cross_entropy*(*output_rref.local_value()*,* target_rref.local_value()*)*

def identity_fn(inp):
    return inp
  
for minibatch, target in data:
    # Use dist autograd context for distributed autograd.
    with dist_autograd.context() as context_id:
        target_rref = rpc.remote("worker1", identity_fn, target)
        output_rref = model(minibatch)
        loss_rref = rpc.remote("worker1", compute_loss, output_rref, target_rref)
        # Can enhance RRef to ensure this calls "dist_autograd.backward" on the last 
        # node in the pipeline.
        loss_rref.backward(context_id)
        dist_optim.step()
```

## Complex Example

In this example, we have two hosts with 8 GPUs each. On each host, we have intra-layer parallelism for the first 4 GPUs and last 4 GPUs and those two groups are connected via pipeline_sync. pipeline_sync itself is wrapped in DDP and the model is replicated across the two hosts. Pseudocode of what this would look like on each host:

```
# RowParallelLinear here is a slight modification of 
# https://fburl.com/6uv0tr07 (https://github.com/facebookresearch/fairscale/blob/e2d8f573f0600e6f9abc370b2b1f800f4b0ecb9e/fairscale/nn/model_parallel/layers.py#L296) to make it more flexible where it can accept 
# an arbitrary set of devices.
layer1 = RowParallelLinear(100, 50, devices=[0, 1, 2, 3])
layer2 = RowParallelLinear(50, 20, devices=[4, 5, 6, 7])
model = torch.distributed.pipeline_sync(
    nn.Sequential(layer1, layer2), 
    chunks = 4)
ddp_model = DDP(model)

# Now run the training loop with ddp_model.
```

## Single Process vs Multi-Process on the same host

The same API can be applied to either single process or multi-process setups on a single host. In the multi-process setup, we can use [RemoteModule](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/distributed/nn/api/remote_module.py#L147) to setup modules on different processes and use [TensorPipe](https://github.com/pytorch/tensorpipe)'s NVLink support to transfer Tensors from one GPU to another.

### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Currently low precision of PyTorch CPU AMP on eager mode is BF16 and it does not support FP16 i.e. torch.half. If we want to add FP16 support on CPU #97068, we need also to extend PyTorch CPU AMP.

This RFC is proposed to extend PyTorch CPU AMP to support both BF16 and FP16 on eager mode so that users can use `torch.cpu.amp.autocast` to set the lower precision data type to `torch.half/torch.bfloat16` and autocast will automatically cast the inputs to float, lower precision data type i.e. FP16/BF16 or make inputs fall through.

### Proposed Implementation:
**Extend autocast to support setting lower precision data type to FP16 on CPU.**

* Extend autocast init method on CPU: 

   Usage of `torch.autocast`:
   Before: `torch.autocast()` only supports setting dtype to torch.bfloat16 on CPU.  if users use `torch.autocast(device_type="cpu", dtype=torch.half)`, autocast will be disabled with the warning: "In CPU autocast, but the target dtype is not supported. Disabling autocast".

    After: users can set dtype=torch.bfloat16 or dtype=torch.half.:
    ```Python
    with torch.autocast(device_type="cpu", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
        ...
    with torch.autocast(device_type="cpu", dtype=torch.half):
        ...
    ```

* Nest behavior of autocast on CPU:

    Nest AMP with mixed torch.bfloat16 and torch.half is not defined yet in PyTorch. For example:
    ```Python
   with torch.autocast(device_type="cpu", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
        ...
        with torch.autocast(device_type="cpu", dtype=torch.half)::
            ...
    ```
    Both BF16 and FP16 are allowed on CUDA, and it also does not handle such usage specially. In addition,  in such case `cache_enabled` will be also enabled by default, and the dtype of cached tensor (e.g., BF16) may be different with the target data type (e.g., FP16 set by nested amp). Ops may report errors with inconsistent data types.

    Nesting AMP with mixed torch.bfloat16 and torch.half seems unreasonable. To simplify things we can disable such mixed usage or give warning and document it.

### Test
* Add test cases for FP16 autocast on CPU.

### Additional context

This RFC depends on FP16 supports of operators https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/97068
